title: Unit and Component Tests
summary: Pick the right level for each test, write unit tests with Vitest, and test components the way users use them with Testing Library.
intro: Every change to an app can break something that used to work, often far from the line you changed. You can open the browser and click through after each edit, but you'll only check what you remember to, and a real app has hundreds of things to check. Teams write tests instead: small programs that check the app for them, in seconds, every time. Testing is new in this course, so this lesson starts from what a test is and why teams rely on them, then explains the kinds of test and how much of each to write. Then it writes real ones for the shop: unit tests with Vitest, component tests with Testing Library, tests that click and type like a user, and tests for components that need providers, hooks, and a fixed clock.

steps.title: What a test is, and why teams write them
steps.body:
Before any tool, it helps to see what a test actually is, because it's simpler than it sounds. You've been testing all along, by hand: you save a file, switch to the browser, and check that the page looks right. An automated test does that checking with code.

## A test checks one fact

A **test** is a small program that runs a piece of your code with an input you chose, and compares what comes back with what you expected. If they match, the test **passes**. If not, it **fails**, and tells you what it got instead. That's all. The shop's `formatPrice` takes a price in cents and returns the text a shopper sees. A test for it says: given `18900`, I expect `"$189.00"`.

```diagram unit-and-component-tests-loop
A test runs your code with a known input and compares the result with what it expected.
```

In step 1 of the diagram, the test calls your code with its input. In step 2 your code returns a result. In step 3 the test compares it with the expected value, and reports pass or fail.

Most tests follow the same three beats, often called **arrange, act, assert**:

1. **Arrange**: set up what the test needs, like some data, or a component on a page.
2. **Act**: do the one thing being tested, like calling a function or clicking a button.
3. **Assert**: check the result. An **assertion** is one claim about it, like this text equals `$189.00`.

## Why teams write them

- **They catch regressions.** A **regression** is something that used to work and broke. Change the price formatting for one page, and a test for another page fails before any shopper sees it.
- **They let you change code without fear.** To **refactor** is to restructure code without changing what it does, like splitting a big component or swapping a library. With tests, you know at once whether you kept the behavior.
- **They're fast.** A test file runs in under a second. Clicking through every case by hand takes minutes, and gets skipped when you're in a hurry.
- **They explain the code.** A test named never goes past 10 of one item tells the next developer a rule that's easy to miss in the code itself.
- **They guard the whole team's work.** CI, the service from the Starting a New React Project lesson that checks every change before it's merged, runs every test too, so a change that fails one can't be merged. Every team you join will have this.

## What a failure looks like

The first example below is the test file, and its output when everything passes. The second shows what happens when someone breaks `formatPrice` with a shortcut: `"$" + cents / 100`. That looks fine for `1999`, which gives `$19.99`, and the test for it still passes. But `18900` becomes `$189` with no cents, and `123456` becomes `$1234.56` with no comma. Two tests fail, and each one says exactly what it expected and what it got, and points at the line.

## What tests cost

Tests are code, so they take time to write and to keep working. A bad test is worse than none: one that fails when nothing is actually wrong teaches the team to ignore failures. The rest of this lesson is about writing the kind that pays for itself, tests that check what the code does for its users, not how it happens to be written.

steps.title: Kinds of test, and how many of each
steps.body:
A test can check one function or the whole app in a real browser. Each kind catches different bugs at a different cost, so teams mix them. Knowing the trade-offs tells you which kind to write for each thing you want to check.

## Four levels

- **Static checks** don't run your code at all. TypeScript's `tsc -b` catches a wrong type or a misspelled property, and a **linter** like oxlint, which the Starting a New React Project lesson set up, catches patterns that are usually bugs, like a hook called inside an `if`. They run in seconds and catch a surprising share of mistakes.
- **Unit tests** check one small piece on its own: a function like `formatPrice`, the cart store, a custom hook. They're the fastest tests and point straight at the broken line.
- **Integration tests** check several pieces working together: a product page with its query, its form, and its error messages, rendered the way the app renders them, with only the network replaced by a stand-in. Component tests with Testing Library, which this lesson starts and the next one finishes, are integration tests.
- **End-to-end tests**, or **e2e**, run the real app in a real browser against a real server, clicking and typing like a person, as the last testing lesson does. They're the most realistic and the slowest, and when one fails, the cause could be anywhere.

## The testing trophy

Moving up the levels, each test is slower, more work to keep running, and more likely to be **flaky**, which means it sometimes fails when nothing is wrong, from timing or a slow network. But each is also closer to what users actually do, so a pass means more. A long-popular picture, the **testing trophy**, suggests how to split your effort:

```diagram unit-and-component-tests-trophy
The widest part, integration, is where most tests give the most confidence for the least effort.
```

Static checks are the base, and cost almost nothing once set up. Unit tests cover logic with many cases. Integration tests are the widest part, since one test checks a whole feature the way a user meets it. A few end-to-end tests sit on top, for the journeys that must never break, like logging in and checking out.

## Test what it does, not how it does it

A test should fail when the app breaks for its users, and only then. So test **behavior**, what a user can see and do, not **implementation details**, the names and structure inside the code that a user never meets:

```tsx
// Tied to how the form is built: breaks if the state is renamed or moved.
expect(form.state.quantity).toBe(3);

// About what a shopper sees: passes after any rewrite that keeps the behavior.
expect(screen.getByLabelText("Quantity")).toHaveValue(3);
```

The first line reaches inside the component. Rename the state or move it to a reducer, and the test fails, though the form works exactly as before. The second line looks at the page the way a person does, through the label they'd read. Testing Library, from part 4 on, is built to make the second kind easy and the first kind hard.

## Where this course tests what

| Level | Tool | In the shop |
|---|---|---|
| Static | `tsc -b`, oxlint | every file, on every build |
| Unit | Vitest | `formatPrice`, the cart store, `useDebouncedValue`, `postedAgo` |
| Integration | Vitest, Testing Library, MSW | `ProductCard`, `AddToCartForm`, then pages with their data in the next lesson |
| End-to-end | Playwright | logging in, adding to the cart, and screenshots, in the course's last lesson |

Test files sit next to the code they test, as the Routing and App Structure lesson's folder layout suggested: `ProductCard.test.tsx` beside `ProductCard.tsx`. Moving a feature moves its tests with it, and a file with no test beside it is easy to spot.

steps.title: Unit tests with Vitest
steps.body:
You need a program that finds your test files, runs them, and reports what failed: a **test runner**. Vitest is the one made for Vite projects. It reads your `vite.config.ts`, so it understands TypeScript, JSX, and the `@/` imports with no extra setup.

## Setting it up

Install Vitest, a fake browser for it, and Testing Library, which the next parts use, as dev dependencies:

```bash
npm install -D vitest jsdom @testing-library/react @testing-library/dom @testing-library/user-event @testing-library/jest-dom
```

Then add a `test` block to `vite.config.ts`. This is the shop's, all of it:

```ts
/// <reference types="vitest/config" />
import babel from "@rolldown/plugin-babel";
import tailwindcss from "@tailwindcss/vite";
import react, { reactCompilerPreset } from "@vitejs/plugin-react";
import { defineConfig } from "vite";

// Requests to /v1 go to the API. API_URL lets a test run point at its own copy.
const api = { "/v1": process.env.API_URL ?? "http://127.0.0.1:4000" };

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [react(), babel({ presets: [reactCompilerPreset()] }), tailwindcss()],
  resolve: { tsconfigPaths: true },
  server: { proxy: api },
  preview: { proxy: api },
  test: {
    environment: "jsdom",
    setupFiles: ["./src/test/setup.ts"],
    include: ["src/**/*.test.{ts,tsx}"],
    exclude: ["src/**/*.browser.test.tsx"],
    coverage: {
      include: ["src/**/*.{ts,tsx}"],
      exclude: ["src/api/gen/**", "src/mocks/**", "src/test/**", "src/main.tsx"],
    },
  },
});
```

The plugins and `resolve` are the ones from Starting a New React Project. The proxy is the one from Routing and App Structure, now reading `API_URL`, so a test run can point it at a copy of the API of its own. The `test` block is new:

- `environment: "jsdom"` runs each test file with **jsdom**, a version of the browser's DOM written in JavaScript that runs inside Node. There's no screen and no layout, but `document`, elements, events, and `localStorage` all work, which is what component tests need.
- `setupFiles` runs `src/test/setup.ts` before each test file. Part 4 fills it in.
- `include` and `exclude` say which files are tests. The browser tests in the course's last lesson use another config, so they're left out here.
- `coverage` is explained at the end of this part.

Add scripts to `package.json`: `"test": "vitest"` and `"test:run": "vitest run"`. `npm test` starts **watch mode**: Vitest runs the tests, then keeps watching your files and reruns the affected tests every time you save, in well under a second. `vitest run` runs everything once and exits, which is what CI uses.

## describe, it, and expect

You've seen the three pieces. `describe` groups tests and can nest. `it`, or its other name `test`, defines one test. `expect` makes an assertion with a **matcher**, the method that says how to compare:

- `toBe(x)` for numbers, strings, and true or false, compared like `===`.
- `toEqual(x)` for objects and arrays, compared by their contents. Two different arrays holding the same items are equal, though `===` says they aren't.
- `toBeUndefined()`, `toBeNull()`, `toContain(item)`, `toHaveLength(n)`, `toThrow()`, and many more.

`.not` turns any of them around: `expect(list).not.toContain("hip-pack-5")`.

## Testing a store

The cart store from the Sharing State lesson is plain JavaScript under the hood: `useCartStore.getState()` returns the state and its actions, with no component needed. The first example tests it. One catch matters everywhere in testing: **tests must not affect each other**. The store is one shared object, so whatever one test adds is still there in the next, and the persisted copy in `localStorage` too. `beforeEach` runs before every test in the `describe`, and resets both. A test that passes alone but fails when run with others is almost always missing a reset like this.

## Coverage

**Coverage** measures which lines of your code ran during the tests. Install `@vitest/coverage-v8` and run `npx vitest run --coverage`. The shop's config lists every source file with `include`, so a file that no test touches shows up at 0 percent instead of being left out. The second example checks the cart store alone and finds two lines no test runs: `removeItem` and `clear`.

Coverage tells you what's untested. It doesn't tell you what's well tested: a line can run in a test that checks nothing about it. So use it to find gaps, and don't chase 100 percent. Teams often set a floor, like 80 percent, that CI won't let drop.

examples.title: Testing the cart store
examples.prompt: `src/features/cart/cartStore.test.ts`. The store is the persisted one from the Sharing State lesson, saved in `localStorage` as `trailhead-cart`, with one addition: `addItem` takes an optional quantity, which the product page uses for a guest.
examples.explanation: `beforeEach` clears `localStorage` and puts the store back to empty, so each test starts the same way. The first test acts through the store's own `addItem`, twice, and `toEqual` checks the whole array by its contents. The second arranges with `setState`, starting at the limit, so it doesn't need ten calls to get there. The third tests the selector from the Sharing State lesson. The last checks what `persist` wrote, with `partialize` leaving `isOpen` out, which is exactly the kind of rule a later change could break without anyone noticing. Jsdom's `localStorage` is real enough for this.

Add a test for each, and the file reaches 100 percent. The coverage report also writes an HTML version in `coverage/`, which shows your code with untested lines in red.

steps.title: Rendering components with Testing Library
steps.body:
Most of a React app is components, and what matters about a component is what shows up on the page and what happens when someone uses it. Testing Library renders a component into jsdom's page and gives you ways to find things on it the way a person would: by what they say and what they're for.

## render and screen

`render(<ProductCard product={tent} />)` from `@testing-library/react` puts the component into `document.body`, the same way `createRoot` does in the app. `screen` then searches the whole page. A component that uses a router hook or `<Link>` needs a router around it, which the `wrapper` option adds: `render(ui, { wrapper: MemoryRouter })`. A **memory router** keeps its location in memory instead of the address bar, which is what tests need.

## Finding things like a user

Testing Library's queries are ordered by how close they are to what people use. Reach for the first one that works:

1. `getByRole("button", { name: "Add Storm Shell Jacket to cart" })` finds an element by its **role**, what it is to assistive technology like a screen reader, and its **accessible name**, what a screen reader says for it. The web course chose HTML elements for their meaning: a `<button>` has the role button, a link has link, an `<h2>` has heading. A name is the button's text, the link's text, or the label of an input.
2. `getByLabelText("Quantity")` finds a form field by its label.
3. `getByText("Out of stock")` finds an element by its text, for things that aren't interactive.
4. `getByTestId("price")` finds an element with a `data-testid` attribute you added just for tests. It's the last resort, since no user ever sees it.

A role query does double duty. If a test can't find your button by its role and name, a screen reader user can't either, so writing these tests checks accessibility for free. The second example shows the message when a role query finds nothing: Testing Library lists every role on the page with its name, which is often the fastest way to see what the component really rendered.

## get, query, and find

Each query comes in three forms, which differ in what happens when the element isn't there:

| Form | If nothing matches | If several match | Use it to |
|---|---|---|---|
| `getBy...` | throws an error | throws an error | find something that must be there now |
| `queryBy...` | returns `null` | throws an error | check that something is not there |
| `findBy...` | keeps trying, then rejects | rejects | wait for something that appears later |

`getAllBy...`, `queryAllBy...`, and `findAllBy...` return arrays, for when you expect several.

## Matchers for the DOM

`@testing-library/jest-dom` adds matchers that read like sentences about the page: `toBeInTheDocument()`, `toHaveTextContent("…")`, `toHaveAttribute("href", "/…")`, `toHaveValue(3)`, `toBeDisabled()`, `toBeVisible()`. Importing `@testing-library/jest-dom/vitest` in the setup file adds them to every `expect`.

## The setup file

The setup file also has to clean up. Every `render` adds to the same `document.body`, and nothing removes it, so the second test in a file would find the first test's card too, and a query that expects one match would throw because it found two. Testing Library can clean up after each test by itself, but only when the test runner's functions are global, which Vitest leaves off unless you ask. So the setup file does it, in an `afterEach`, which runs after every test:

```ts
import "@testing-library/jest-dom/vitest";
import { cleanup } from "@testing-library/react";
import { afterEach } from "vitest";

// Unmount whatever each test rendered, so the next one starts from an empty page.
afterEach(() => {
  cleanup();
});
```

The next lesson adds a few lines to this file for the network.

The third uses `queryByText`, since `getByText` would throw before `expect` could check anything, and asserts the badge is not there. None of the tests mention the `card` class name or the `

steps.title: Acting like a user
steps.body:
Rendering checks what a component shows. Most bugs, though, live in what it does when someone clicks, types, or presses Enter, so tests have to do those things too, the way a person would.

## user-event

`@testing-library/user-event` acts out what a person does, one real step at a time. `user.type(input, "3")` doesn't just set the value: it focuses the input, then fires the key down, key press, input, and key up events for each character, the same events a keyboard makes. So the component's handlers run exactly as they would for a real shopper, bugs included.

Start each test with `const user = userEvent.setup()`, then `await` each action, since they're asynchronous:

- `await user.click(element)` moves the pointer there, presses, and releases.
- `await user.type(element, "text")` clicks into it and types.
- `await user.clear(element)` selects everything in a field and deletes it.
- `await user.keyboard("{Enter}")` presses keys on whatever has focus. Names in braces are special keys: `{Tab}`, `{Escape}`, `{ArrowDown}`.
- `await user.selectOptions(select, "3")` picks an option.

Testing Library also has `fireEvent`, which fires one single event. It's lower level and skips the steps a real browser would take, so prefer `user-event`.

## Checking what was called

`AddToCartForm` from the shop doesn't add anything itself: it calls the `onAdd` function its parent passes, with the quantity. To check that, the test passes a **mock function**, `vi.fn()` from Vitest, a stand-in that does nothing but remember every call and its arguments. Then `expect(onAdd).toHaveBeenCalledWith(3)` checks how it was called, and `toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1)` how often, so a double submit would fail the test. A mock function is one kind of **test double**, anything that stands in for real code during a test.

## A bug only a user would find

The second example is a real bug these tests caught. An earlier version of `AddToCartForm` kept the quantity as a number and turned an empty box back into `1` as soon as it was cleared. Clicking through by hand, it seemed fine: the box starts at 1, and the arrows change it. But a shopper who selects the 1, deletes it, and types 3 gets 13, since the 1 comes back the moment the box is empty, and 13 is over the limit of 10, so the browser refuses to submit. The test does exactly what that shopper does, `clear`, then `type`, and the failure says it plainly: expected 3, received 13.

The fix, in the first example's component, keeps the box's text as a string and only turns it into a number on submit. A unit test of the state wouldn't have found this, since each piece worked alone. It took a test that acts like a person.

## Waiting for things

When something changes after an action, a request or a timer, the page isn't ready the moment `click` returns. `findBy...` queries wait for you, retrying for up to a second by default: `expect(await screen.findByText("Added to your cart.")).toBeInTheDocument()`. For a check that isn't a query, `waitFor` retries a whole callback until it passes or times out:

```tsx
await waitFor(() => expect(onSearch).toHaveBeenCalledWith("tent"));
```

Never wait with a fixed delay like a `setTimeout` of half a second: it's too slow when the app is fast and too short when the computer is busy, which is how tests become flaky.

## What act warnings mean

Sometimes a test passes but prints a warning that an update was not wrapped in `act(...)`. React batches the updates from an event and applies them inside `act`, and Testing Library wraps `render`, `user-event`, and its waiting queries in it for you. The warning means a state update happened after the test stopped watching, usually because the test didn't wait for something the component was still doing. The fix is almost never to add `act` yourself: await the `findBy...` query, or the `waitFor`, for the change that caused the update.

examples.title: Testing the add-to-cart form
examples.explanation: Each test makes its own `user` and its own `onAdd`, so no calls leak from one test to the next. The first test does what a shopper does and checks two things: the box shows 3, and `onAdd` got 3, once. The second clicks into the box and presses Enter, which submits the form, as it would in a browser, and the default of 1 is sent. The third renders the form disabled and finds its button with a **regular expression**, a pattern for matching text, `/add storm shell/i`, where `i` ignores capital letters. Clicking a disabled button does nothing, so `onAdd` is never called.

examples.explanation: `valueAsNumber || 1` is the bug. When the shopper clears the box, `valueAsNumber` is `NaN`, the not-a-number value JavaScript uses for an empty number field, and `NaN || 1` gives `1`, so React puts the 1 straight back. Typing 3 after it makes 13. The failing assertion is the one about what the shopper sees, `toHaveValue(3)`, and the output points at it with the received value, so the cause is easy to guess. The fixed component keeps the raw text in state with `useState("1")`, which lets the box be empty while someone types, and turns it into a number with `Number(quantity)` only when the form is submitted.

steps.title: Providers, hooks, and a fixed clock
steps.body:
Real components lean on things around them: a query client for server data, a router for links and params, stores, and the clock. A test has to supply each one, fresh, so that every test starts from the same place. This part sets up the helpers the next lesson uses for whole pages.

## A custom render

The shop's pages call `useQuery`, which needs a `QueryClientProvider` above them, and `useParams`, which needs a router. Wrapping each test by hand gets repetitive, so teams write one helper, usually in `src/test/render.tsx`. The first example is the shop's. `renderWithProviders(<ProductPage />, { path: "/products/:slug", route: "/products/storm-shell-jacket" })` renders the page inside a new query client and a memory router that starts at that URL, so `useParams` returns `storm-shell-jacket`.

Each call makes a **new** `QueryClient`, for the same reason the cart store gets reset: TanStack Query caches data in the client, and a cache shared between tests would let one test see another's data. Its settings fit tests:

- `retry: false`. In the app, a failed query is retried three times with growing waits, which would make every error test take seconds. In a test, one failure is the answer.
- `gcTime: Infinity`. Garbage collection, which removes unused data from the cache after a while, does nothing useful in a short test and would leave a timer running after it.

It also creates the `user` for `user-event`, so tests write `const { user } = renderWithProviders(...)`. There's a second helper, `renderApp(route)`, which renders the app's real list of routes, header and all, for tests of whole pages. For that, the route objects from the Routing and App Structure lesson move into a file of their own, `src/app/routes.tsx`, which `router.tsx` and the tests both import.

## Testing a hook

A custom hook can't be called outside a component, so `renderHook` from Testing Library renders a tiny one that calls it and hands you the result. `result.current` is what the hook returned in the latest render, and `rerender(newProps)` renders again with new arguments. The second example tests `useDebouncedValue` from the Effects, Refs, and Browser APIs lesson, which only catches up with its value after a pause.

## Fake timers

That pause is 300 milliseconds, and a test that really waited would be slow and could be flaky. `vi.useFakeTimers()` replaces `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, and `Date` with fakes that only move when you say. `vi.advanceTimersByTime(299)` moves the fake clock forward 299 milliseconds instantly, running any timer that comes due. Moving the clock makes the hook set state, so the test does it inside `act(...)`, from `@testing-library/react`, which applies the update before the next assertion. This is the one place you'll write `act` yourself: when the test itself causes the update, by moving time.

Call `vi.useRealTimers()` in an `afterEach`, or the fake clock leaks into every test that runs after it.

## A fixed clock

Anything that reads the current date gives a different answer every day, which makes its output impossible to check. `vi.setSystemTime(date)` sets the fake clock to a moment you choose, so `Date.now()` and `new Date()` return it. The third example tests `postedAgo`, which turns a review's date into words like yesterday, with the clock set to `2026-10-01T09:00:00Z`. That's the same moment the Trailhead API's seed data uses, so dates in mocked responses and the test's now agree.

## Resetting everything

Before each test, every shared thing should be back where it started. In the shop:

- The DOM: `cleanup()` in the setup file, after each test.
- Server data: a new `QueryClient` in every `renderWithProviders` call.
- Stores: `useCartStore.setState(...)` and `localStorage.clear()` in `beforeEach`.
- Time: `vi.useRealTimers()` in `afterEach`, wherever a file uses fake timers.
- Mock functions: a new `vi.fn()` in each test, or `vi.restoreAllMocks()` in `afterEach`.

Get this right, and tests can run in any order, alone or together, and give the same result. That's the property that lets Vitest run test files in parallel, and lets you trust a failure when you see one.

The tests in this lesson never touch the network. The next lesson, Mocking APIs With MSW and Kubb, gives them an API to talk to: a fake one you control, built from the real one's spec.

examples.title: A render with every provider
examples.prompt: `src/test/render.tsx`, the shop's test helpers. Tests import them as `@/test/render`.
examples.explanation: `createMemoryRouter` takes a route list and `initialEntries`, the history the memory router starts with. `renderWithProviders` builds a one-route list around the component you pass, with your `path`, so params work. `renderApp` uses the real `routes` instead, so a test can start at `/cart` and see the header, the layout, and the cart page together. Both return everything `render` does, plus `user`, the `queryClient`, and the `router`, so a test can check `router.state.location.pathname` after a click, or look in the cache. `createTestQueryClient` is exported for tests that need to fill the cache before rendering.

examples.title: Testing a debounced value
examples.prompt: `src/hooks/useDebouncedValue.test.ts`, for the hook from the Effects, Refs, and Browser APIs lesson.
examples.explanation: `renderHook` calls the hook with `initialProps`, so the first value is `ten`. `rerender` changes it to `tent`, as if the shopper typed one more letter, and the debounced value is still `ten`, since no time has passed. After 299 fake milliseconds it still hasn't changed. One more millisecond fires the timer, the hook sets its state inside `act`, and `result.current` is `tent`. The whole test took 7 milliseconds of real time. Without fake timers it would have to really wait, and the check at 299 would be a race against the computer's own speed.

examples.title: Testing dates with a fixed clock
examples.prompt: `src/lib/dates.test.ts`, for `postedAgo` in `src/lib/dates.ts`, which uses `Intl.RelativeTimeFormat` to say how long ago a date was.
examples.explanation: `beforeEach` turns on fake timers and sets the clock to the seed data's moment, so inside each test, now is always nine in the morning on October 1, 2026. A day before that comes out as yesterday, because the formatter's `numeric: "auto"` uses words where it can, and a week before as 7 days ago. Run this a year from now, and it still passes. Without the fixed clock, both tests would have broken the day after they were written. `afterEach` puts the real clock back, so the next file that reads the time gets the real one.

recap:
- A test runs your code with a known input and checks the result: arrange, act, assert.
- Tests catch regressions, let you refactor safely, and run in CI on every push.
- Static checks, unit, integration, and end-to-end tests trade speed for realism, and integration tests give the most for the effort.
- Test behavior a user can see, not implementation details.
- Vitest runs tests with `describe`, `it`, and `expect`, in jsdom, in watch mode, with coverage to find gaps.
- Testing Library finds elements by role and name first, with `getBy`, `queryBy`, and `findBy` for present, absent, and later.
- `user-event` acts like a person, `vi.fn()` records calls, and `findBy` or `waitFor` wait instead of fixed delays.
- Give every test fresh providers, stores, timers, and mocks, so tests pass in any order.
